measures.questionText: Pursuant to the Arizona State Constitution, Pima County seeks voter approval to permanently adjust the expenditure base of the County as determined by the Economic Estimates Commission. The County seeks an adjustment of $70,000,000. A “YES” vote shall have the effect of allowing Pima County to adjust its 1979-80 base expenditure limit. A “NO” vote shall have the effect of not allowing Pima County to adjust its 1979-80 base expenditure limit.
measures.officialStatement: Official Title: A resolution proposing a permanent adjustment to the state-imposed 1979-80 expenditure base for Pima County. Summary analysis: if approved, the County’s 1979-80 base expenditure limitation will be increased by $70,000,000 adjusted each future year for population and inflation growth since 1979-80. With voter approval, in fiscal year 2027-2028 the County’s expenditure limitation will increase by $610,086,481, from $817,131,286 to $1,427,217,767. Referred to the people by the Pima County Board of Supervisors by resolution 2026-23, passed 2026-04-21.

scopedCoverageNotes.text: Proposition 427, a $250,000,000 bond for Pima County Joint Technical Education District No. 11, is on the ballot of every voter in that district — which includes all of ZIP 85641 — and is not shown as a contest because no division in this registry matches the district's territory. Measured 2026-08-27 against the county's own JTED layer: the district covers about 73% of Pima County AND contains sampled points in Pinal County, so attaching it to the county would both show it to voters who do not vote on it and hide it from voters who do. Its estimated average tax rate is $0.14 per $100 of net assessed limited property value; its question text is not published — the district's Request for Arguments says the text is available by request from the district at 2855 West Master Pieces Drive, Tucson.

Justice of the Peace and Constable are elected by justice precinct, and this registry has no justice-precinct division. ZIP 85641 spans Precincts 7 and 8. On the November 3, 2026 ballot, Precinct 7 elects a Justice of the Peace (Raymond Carroll won the Republican primary 7,077 to Kara Egbert's 4,773; no Democrat filed) and Precinct 8 elects a Justice of the Peace (Kristel Ann Foster, Democratic, and William Parven, Republican). Neither precinct has a Constable race this cycle: the only Constable contests on the county's official candidate list are Precincts 2, 3 and 9.

Pima County's elected county offices — Sheriff, Assessor, Recorder, Treasurer, County Attorney, School Superintendent — and Board of Supervisors Districts 2 and 4 are NOT on the November 3, 2026 ballot. This is read from the county's Official Candidate List, which prints uncontested races and lists only Board of Supervisors District 5 among supervisor seats; it is not a gap in this file.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Would change the Arizona Constitution so the state and its cities, towns, and counties can't charge a tax or fee based on how many miles you drive, and can't track or limit your driving miles unless you agree to it. It wouldn't cover government vehicles, or commercial trucks that cross state lines under an interstate fuel-tax agreement.

parts.label: No tax or fee based on miles driven
parts.what: The state, and any county, city, town or other local government, could not charge a tax or fee based on the number of miles a person drives.

parts.label: No tracking your miles without your consent
parts.what: Those same governments could not monitor or limit how many miles a person drives unless that person voluntarily agrees to it.

parts.label: Two exceptions
parts.what: It would not cover commercial vehicles that operate in more than one state where an interstate agreement exists for reporting fuel taxes or registration fees, and it would not cover vehicles owned and operated by the state or a local government.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Would change the Arizona Constitution so state and local governments — including public schools, universities, and community colleges — can't favor or disadvantage anyone based on race, sex, color, ethnicity, or national origin in public jobs, education, or contracting. It would also bar them from making people state support for race-based diversity, equity, and inclusion ideas to get a job, admission, or a scholarship; bar spending public money on offices at public schools whose role is promoting race-based preferential treatment; and bar discipline policies that treat students or employees differently by race or ethnicity. The proposition lists specific exceptions.

parts.label: No preferences and no discrimination by race, sex or national origin
parts.what: The state, cities, towns, counties, public universities, community colleges, school districts and other local governments could not give preferential treatment to, or discriminate against, people or groups based on race, sex, color, ethnicity or national origin in public employment, education or contracting — even where it is part of a federal program.

parts.label: No required statements of support
parts.what: They could not require applicants, employees, students or contractors to endorse or support race-based preferential treatment as a condition of admission, graduation, hiring, promotion, certification, contracting or a scholarship. That includes asking someone for a written or spoken statement supporting the race-based diversity, equity and inclusion ideas the measure identifies, asking them to confess race-based privilege or discuss their own or others' race, preferring someone for opinions they expressed if those opinions are based on race or ethnicity, and requiring a training or course that promotes those ideas.

parts.label: No public money for offices that promote preferences
parts.what: They could not spend public money to run or contract for an office or position at a public school, college or university whose job is promoting preferential treatment or discrimination based on race or ethnicity — including spending to influence who is on the faculty or in the student body, or on trainings, programs, activities and policies designed with reference to race, ethnicity, intersectionality, gender identity or sexual orientation, except as the measure otherwise provides.

parts.label: No discipline policies that differ by race
parts.what: They could not use any disciplinary policy or practice that treats students or employees differently on the basis of race or ethnicity.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Would change the Arizona Constitution so school districts can't use public money, staff time, or district communication systems to support unions, and can't take union dues out of employees' paychecks. Each school district employee would negotiate their own pay, benefits, and working conditions — the state and school districts would be barred from negotiating with a union on employees' behalf. It would override existing agreements and take effect January 1, 2028.

parts.label: No public money or resources for union operations
parts.what: A school district could not use public money or public resources to support a labor organization's operations, and could not use them to carry out labor organization activities during working hours.

parts.label: No union dues taken out of a paycheck
parts.what: A school district could not deduct any payment for labor organization membership dues from an employee's paycheck.

parts.label: No district communication systems for union material
parts.what: A school district could not give access to its internal communications systems to distribute labor organization recruiting information or political materials, and district employees could not distribute written, printed or digital communications on a labor organization's behalf in a way that uses public resources.

parts.label: Each employee negotiates for themselves
parts.what: Every school district employee would have the right to negotiate their own pay, benefits and working conditions, and the state and its local governments could not negotiate an agreement with a labor organization about school district employees' terms and conditions of employment.

parts.label: Existing agreements would be overridden
parts.what: It would supersede any school district contract, memorandum of understanding, meet-and-confer agreement, policy, ordinance or other written or spoken agreement.

parts.label: Starts January 1, 2028
parts.what: The measure would apply beginning January 1, 2028.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Would change the Arizona Constitution on elections: only U.S. citizens could register and vote; voters would show valid government-issued ID before casting a ballot in every election; voters would get the option to have their ballot counted at their voting place on election day; and foreign nationals couldn't spend money to influence Arizona elections. It would let the legislature and the voters pass election laws — including on early and mail voting — if the laws are rationally connected to a legitimate state interest, and would apply to elections from January 1, 2028.

parts.label: Only U.S. citizens may register and vote
parts.what: It would reaffirm that only United States citizens may register to vote and vote in Arizona elections, and that Arizona elections are decided solely by the votes of eligible citizen voters.

parts.label: Government-issued ID before casting a ballot
parts.what: Voters would have to present valid government-issued proof of identity before casting a ballot in every election, as prescribed by law.

parts.label: The option to have your ballot counted where you vote
parts.what: Voters would have to be given the option to have their ballot tabulated at their voting location on election day.

parts.label: No foreign money in Arizona elections
parts.what: Foreign nationals could not contribute or spend money or anything of value to influence an Arizona election, and no person could accept such a contribution.

parts.label: A standard future election laws would have to meet
parts.what: The people and the legislature could pass laws governing elections, including early voting and mail voting, if those laws are rationally connected to a legitimate state interest — the measure names timely and accurate results, efficient election administration, election security, and preserving public confidence in election integrity.

parts.label: The legislature would have to pay for it
parts.what: The legislature would be required to appropriate any money necessary to carry the measure out.

parts.label: Applies to elections from January 1, 2028
parts.what: It would apply to all elections taking place on or after January 1, 2028.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Would change the Arizona Constitution so the state can't take money out of a state-run scholarship account belonging to the child of a military family — someone serving on active duty, or killed in the line of duty — where the account can pay tuition at universities, community colleges, or accredited private colleges. Any later law violating this rule would be entirely void. Closing an account for reasons like illegal activity, choosing to close it, graduating, or not enrolling for four years after high school wouldn't count as taking the money.

parts.label: The state could not take back the money
parts.what: The state could not seize, transfer or otherwise take money from the scholarship account of a child of a military family — a child of someone serving or who has served on active duty, or who was killed in the line of duty — where the program is run by the state, treats such children who meet enrollment requirements as eligible, and lets the money be used for tuition or fees at state universities, community colleges, or private accredited colleges.

parts.label: A later law that breaks this would be void
parts.what: If the legislature passes a bill, or voters pass a ballot measure, on or after November 1, 2026 that violates those protections, the entire bill or measure would be void.

parts.label: What would not count as taking the money
parts.what: Closing an account because of illegal activity, closing it voluntarily, not renewing it, graduating from a college, or not enrolling in one for at least four years after finishing high school would not count as taking the money.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Would change Arizona's school-voucher (ESA) program. Starting in the 2027–2028 school year, families making over $150,000 a year couldn't join (children with disabilities, and children eligible before 2022, excepted). Unspent account money would be transferred out each year, mostly to a classroom fund. Schools, tutoring businesses, and individual tutors would have to register with the state, pay annual fees, and fingerprint staff who are alone with students before being paid with ESA money — and ESA money couldn't buy items designated noneducational or luxury goods. The Attorney General would enforce the rules, and the committee that sponsored the proposition could sue participating families and schools over violations.

parts.label: A $150,000 family income limit
parts.what: From the 2027-2028 school year, children who would otherwise qualify but whose annual family income is over $150,000 — adjusted each year, or a lower figure set by the legislature — could not enrol in the empowerment scholarship account program. The limit would apply no matter how many children are in a family, and would not apply to children who would have been eligible before 2022, including children with disabilities.

parts.label: An unrenewed account closes after one year
parts.what: An account would stay open for one school year rather than three if the parent does not renew the contract.

parts.label: Leftover account money moves to the classroom site fund
parts.what: Each July 1 the Arizona Department of Education would take whatever money is left in a student's account and transfer 90 percent of it to the classroom site fund — every two years rather than yearly for a student with a disability — with a portion going to the Department or the State Board of Education to carry out and enforce the measure.

parts.label: The sponsoring committee could sue families and schools
parts.what: The political action committee that sponsored the measure would have the power to sue the families and private schools taking part in the program over any violations of it.

parts.label: Permanent disqualification for intentional misspending
parts.what: A parent, student or account holder found to have intentionally misspent account money would be permanently barred from the program, the account would be closed, and any money left in it returned to the state.

parts.label: Quarterly public reports and Attorney General enforcement
parts.what: The Department of Education would file quarterly reports with the attorney general and post each one on its website. The attorney general would enforce the rules for the money, and anything recovered as restitution would go into the classroom site fund.

parts.label: Removes a court protection for participating schools
parts.what: It would repeal today's requirement that, when a state law about the program is challenged in court, the state must prove the challenged law is necessary and does not put an undue burden on qualified schools.

parts.label: New limits on what the money can be spent on
parts.what: Tuition and fees could only go to schools that register with the Department and meet requirements including fingerprinting staff who have unsupervised contact with students and disclosing testing. Tutoring and teaching could only be bought from a registered qualified tutor, or through a school, business or accredited facility at a registered location. The supplemental materials that can be bought would change; items designated non-educational or luxury goods could not be bought at all; and unless the student has a disability, the money could not be paid to a member of the student's family.

parts.label: Annual registration for schools, providers and tutors
parts.what: From July 1, 2027, schools, tutoring providers and individual tutors would register each campus or location with the Department every year, pay an annual registration fee, and show they meet safety, location, non-discrimination, accreditation and fingerprint requirements. They would be subject to the same laws on investigating and disciplining misconduct that apply to public school employees. Families could not be reimbursed for payments to anyone unregistered, and registration forms and supporting documents would be public records.

parts.label: $1,750,000 moved from the medical marijuana fund
parts.what: On the day the measure takes effect, $1,750,000 would move from the medical marijuana fund — which has paid for clinical research, the Arizona teachers academy, public health initiatives, substance abuse prevention and administrative costs — to the Department of Education, the State Board of Education, the Department of Public Safety and the attorney general, for the administrative spending the measure requires.

parts.label: The rest survives if part is struck down
parts.what: If any part of the measure is found invalid, the rest would be unaffected, and the invalid parts would be interpreted as far as the law allows.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Would limit city and town taxes on groceries — food and sealed nonalcoholic drinks meant for home use. New grocery taxes and any rate increases would need voter approval and couldn't go above two percent; a city already at two percent or more couldn't raise its rate at all; and no new grocery tax or increase could happen between June 30, 2025 and June 30, 2027.

parts.label: Existing food taxes capped, and some frozen outright
parts.what: A city, town or other taxing jurisdiction that approved a tax or fee on food and certain ready-to-drink non-alcoholic beverages in closed containers for home consumption on or before January 1, 2025 could only raise the rate with voter approval, and never above two percent of the tax base. If the rate on that date was already two percent or more, it could not be raised at all.

parts.label: A new food tax would need a vote
parts.what: A city, town or other taxing jurisdiction that had not approved such a tax or fee on or before January 1, 2025 would need voter approval to adopt one and to raise it afterwards, and it could not be more than two percent of the tax base.

parts.label: A freeze from June 30, 2025 to June 30, 2027
parts.what: No new tax or fee could be adopted and no rate could be increased between June 30, 2025 and June 30, 2027.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Would declare that drug cartels — groups engaged in human smuggling, drug trafficking for profit, or terrorism — are terrorist organizations, and would require the Arizona Department of Homeland Security to use all lawful means within its authority to address threats they pose. It states that it does not support an asylum claim under federal law.

parts.label: Declares drug cartels terrorist organizations
parts.what: It would declare that drug cartels — associations of people engaged in human smuggling, drug trafficking for profit, or any act of terrorism — are terrorist organizations.

parts.label: The state homeland security department would have to act
parts.what: It would require the Arizona Department of Homeland Security to use all lawful means available within its authority to address the threats drug cartels pose.

parts.label: Not a basis for an asylum claim
parts.what: It would declare that the measure does not support a person's claim for asylum under federal law.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Would require school and college sports teams in Arizona to be designated male, female, coeducational, or mixed, and would prohibit athletes whose original birth certificate records them as male from playing on female teams. Restrooms, locker rooms, and shower rooms tied to athletics could only be used according to the sex recorded on the athlete's original birth certificate. It would also expand who can sue over alleged violations.

parts.label: Female sports limited by sex recorded at birth
parts.what: Males could not play in female interscholastic and intramural sports, decided by the biological sex of the athletes as recorded at birth on their original birth certificates.

parts.label: Every team would have to be labeled
parts.what: Public and private schools and athletic associations that sponsor an interscholastic or intramural team or sport would have to expressly designate it as “males”, “men”, “boys”, “females”, “women”, “girls”, “coeducational” or “mixed”.

parts.label: Locker rooms and restrooms by sex recorded at birth
parts.what: Public schools, private schools, higher education institutions and athletic associations that provide private spaces integral to athletics — restrooms, locker rooms and shower rooms — could not authorise anyone to use a space not designated for their biological sex as recorded at birth on their original birth certificate.

parts.label: More people could sue and be sued
parts.what: It would expand who may sue and be sued over alleged violations of the law.

parts.label: Matching and coed teams unaffected
parts.what: It would not restrict any athlete's eligibility to play on a team or in a sport that matches their sex, or one designated coeducational or mixed. “Athlete” would cover students and any individual who takes part in a team or sport.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Would ban speed and red-light cameras (photo enforcement) unless a local government already has a camera contract in place before December 31, 2026. A local government with an existing contract would have to ask its voters at the next general election whether to keep the cameras: a no vote shuts them down within 90 days; a yes vote keeps them for 10 years, with a fresh vote every 10 years after that.

parts.label: No photo enforcement without an existing contract
parts.what: A local authority or state agency could not use a photo enforcement system for speeding or traffic control device violations unless it had a contract in place before December 31, 2026 to operate one.

parts.label: Existing systems would go to the voters
parts.what: A local authority with a contract in place before that date would have to ask voters at the next general election whether it may keep operating the system. If voters say no, it would have to stop within 90 days of the election.

parts.label: Ten years, then another vote
parts.what: If voters approve, the system could keep running for ten years. At the end of each ten-year period the local authority would have to go back to the voters for another ten.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Would require large Arizona school districts — 7,500 or more students, or any district with a school in a county of 500,000 or more people — to spend at least 60 percent of their operating money on direct classroom instruction, with the state auditor general defining the terms. Districts below that line would have to raise the share each year, and districts that don't comply would lose part, and eventually all, of their classroom site fund allocation unless granted a waiver.

parts.label: At least 60 percent spent on classroom instruction
parts.what: Every school district with at least 7,500 students, or that runs a school in a county of at least 500,000 people, would have to spend at least 60 percent of its operational spending on direct instructional expenses.

parts.label: The auditor general would write the definitions
parts.what: The auditor general would define what “direct instructional expenses” and “operational spending” mean for this requirement.

parts.label: Half a percent a year to catch up
parts.what: From the 2027-2028 fiscal year, a district spending less than 60 percent would have to raise the share it spends on direct instruction by at least half of one percent a year until it complies.

parts.label: Classroom site fund money withheld for non-compliance
parts.what: A district that does not comply would lose 25 percent of its classroom site fund allocation for each year it did not comply, up to the whole allocation after four or more years, unless a waiver is granted. The money not distributed would go to complying districts the following school year.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Would let Pima County permanently raise the state-set limit on how much money it is allowed to spend — its “expenditure base” — by $70 million, with that amount adjusted every year afterward for population growth and inflation. The county says that if voters approve it, the spending limit for 2027–28 would rise by about $610 million, from about $817 million to about $1.43 billion. A YES vote lets the county raise its 1979–80 base limit; a NO vote does not. The Pima County Board of Supervisors put it on the ballot.

Would let the Vail Unified School District keep spending up to 12.5% more than the state's revenue control limit each year, for 2027/2028 and the next six years. The district says this continues about $5.1 million above the alternate budget for 2027/2028, at an estimated $1.61 per $100 of a property's secondary assessed value. A YES vote continues the override; a NO vote ends it.

Would let the Sahuarita Unified School District keep spending up to 15% more than its normal day-to-day “maintenance and operations” budget. Only voters who live in the district decide it, at the November 3, 2026 election. A YES vote continues that extra spending; a NO vote ends it.

Would let the Tanque Verde Unified School District keep spending up to 15% more than its normal day-to-day “maintenance and operations” budget. Only voters who live in the district decide it, at the November 3, 2026 election. A YES vote continues that extra spending; a NO vote ends it.

Prohibit foreign nationals from contributing or expending money or anything of value to influence an Arizona election and any person from accepting such a contribution. 6. Allow the people and the legislature to enact laws governing elections, including early voting and mail voting, if the laws are rationally connected to a legitimate state interest, including timely and accurate election results, efficient election administration, election security and preservation of public confidence in election integrity. 7. Require the legislature to appropriate any money necessary to implement this proposition. 8. Apply this proposition to all elections that take place on or after January 1, 2028. 9. Designate this proposition as the "Fast Accurate Secure Transparent Election Results Act" or the "Fast Election Results Act."

analyses.text: - 1 - PROPOSITION ___ [HCR 2048 - 2026] military families; scholarship accounts ANALYSIS BY LEGISLATIVE COUNCIL Proposition ___ would amend the Arizona Constitution to prohibit this state from confiscating (seizing, transferring or otherwise taking) monies from the scholarship account of a child of a military family (the child of a person who is or was serving on active duty or who was killed in the line of duty) if the scholarship account program: 1. Is operated by this state and, at least in part, designates any student who is a child of a military family and who satisfies enrollment requirements as being eligible to receive scholarship monies. 2. Allows the student to use the scholarship account monies for tuition or fees at state universities, community colleges or other postsecondary educational institutions that are private and accredited. Proposition ___ would also provide that if any law is enacted as a bill by the legislature or as a ballot measure by the voters on or after November 1, 2026 and that law violates the military families scholarship account provisions described above, the entire bill or ballot measure is void. Proposition ___ would specify that scholarship account closures based on illegal activity, voluntary closure or nonrenewal, graduation from a postsecondary educational institution or nonenrollment in a postsecondary educational institution for at least four years after graduating from high school are not considered to be a confiscation in violation of this section of the Arizona Constitution. Proposition ___ would designate this proposition as the "Military Families College Savings and Scholarship Protection Act."

- 1 - PROPOSITION ___ [I-09-2026] Protect Education Act ANALYSIS BY LEGISLATIVE COUNCIL Proposition __ would define Arizona ESA monies (ESA monies) to include both current empowerment scholarship accounts (ESA) and any other public monies that may be provided by this state for the purpose of obtaining a nonpublic education, nonpublic educational services or related educational materials for a student eligible to enroll in a public school, with some exceptions. Beginning in the 2027-2028 school year, Proposition ___ would exclude from eligibility in the Arizona empowerment scholarship account program (program) children who would qualify under this existing program but whose annual family income exceeds $150,000, adjusted annually or a lesser amount determined by the legislature. The family income limit would apply regardless of the number of children in a family, but it would not apply to children who would have been eligible to enroll in the program before 2022, including children with disabilities. Proposition ____ would also: 1. Reduce the number of school years that an ESA will remain open, from three school years to one school year, if the qualified student's parent fails to renew the ESA contract. 2. On July 1 of each year, require the Arizona Department of Education (ADE) to take all ESA monies remaining in a qualified student's account as of that date and transfer 90 percent to the classroom site fund (except that ESA monies remaining in the ESA of a qualified student with a disability shall be taken and transferred every two years); a portion of transferred ESA monies shall be transferred to ADE or the State Board of Education (SBE) to implement and enforce the proposition; and the political action committee that sponsored the proposition has the power to sue the families and private schools that participate in the program for any violations of the proposition. 3. Permanently disqualify a parent, qualified student or account holder who is found to have intentionally misspent monies in an ESA from participating in the program and require ADE to close the ESA at issue and return any ESA monies remaining in the ESA to this state in the same manner as the monies described above. 4. Require ADE to submit quarterly reports to the attorney general and to post each report on ADE's website. Additionally, the attorney general would enforce requirements for ESA monies and monies recovered as restitution would be deposited in the classroom site fund. 5. Repeal the requirement under current law that, in a legal proceeding challenging the application of state laws establishing the program to a qualified school, this state must prove that the challenged law is necessary and does not impose any undue burden on qualified schools. Proposition ____ would make the following changes to how monies in a qualified student's ESA and any other ESA monies may be used: 1. Limit the qualified schools at which a qualified student or parent may use ESA monies to pay tuition and fees to only those qualified schools that register with ADE and meet certain requirements, including fingerprinting of teaching and other school personnel who have unsupervised contact with students and testing disclosure.
- 2 - 2. Limit the tutoring and teaching services that may be purchased using ESA monies to only those services that are provided either by a qualified tutor who is registered with ADE and who meets certain prescribed qualifications, including fingerprinting, or by a qualified tutor through a qualified school, business or facility that is accredited by a state, regional or national accrediting organization and is at a location or campus that is registered with ADE. 3. Modify the supplemental materials that a qualified student or parent may purchase using ESA monies. 4. Prohibit qualified students and parents from using ESA monies to pay for items designated as noneducational items or luxury goods. 5. If a qualified student is not a child with a disability, prohibit the qualified student or parent from using ESA monies to pay a member of the qualified student's family. Beginning July 1, 2027, Proposition _____ would: 1. Require a qualified school to annually register with ADE each campus that is operated by the qualified school in order to receive ESA monies. To register, the qualified school would pay an annual registration fee and submit evidence that the qualified school complies with student and site safety rules adopted by SBE and satisfies requirements related to location and nondiscrimination. A qualified school must also be accredited, implement specified testing or serve only children with disabilities. 2. Require an accredited business or facility that provides tutoring or teaching services to annually register with ADE each location that is operated by the qualified tutoring service provider in order to receive ESA monies. To register, the qualified tutoring service provider would pay an annual registration fee and certify that the qualified tutoring service provider employs qualified tutors and requires all personnel who have unsupervised contact with students to have valid fingerprint clearance cards. 3. Provide that all qualified schools and qualified tutoring service providers are subject to specific laws relating to employment by public schools in this state, including laws relating to the investigation of and discipline for acts of immoral or unprofessional conduct that are committed by school employees. 4. Require a qualified tutor who provides tutoring and teaching services outside of a qualified school or qualified tutoring service provider to annually register with ADE to receive ESA monies. To register, the qualified tutor would pay an annual registration fee, submit a copy of the qualified tutor's fingerprint clearance card and certify that the qualified tutor is not subject to disciplinary action by SBE or by a facility that is accredited by a state, regional or national accrediting organization. 5. Provide that all qualified tutors who do not have a valid teaching certificate issued by SBE are subject to specific laws relating to employment of noncertificated personnel by public schools in this state, including laws relating to the investigation of and discipline for acts of immoral or unprofessional conduct that are committed by noncertificated school employees. 6. Require ADE to notify each qualified school, qualified tutoring service provider and qualified tutor that registers with ADE of all program requirements under state law. 7. Provide that a qualified student or parent may not be reimbursed from the qualified student's ESA for payments made to a qualified school, qualified tutoring service provider or qualified tutor that is not registered with ADE. 8. Require each qualified school, qualified tutoring service provider and qualified tutor, before receiving any ESA monies, to be registered with ADE and be included on any platform that ADE provides to qualified students and parents for the purchase of goods or educational
- 3 - services using ESA monies. 9. Provide that all registration forms and supporting documents are public records. Proposition ____ would also: 1. On the proposition's effective date, transfer a total of $1,750,000 from the medical marijuana fund, which has been used to fund clinical research, the Arizona teachers academy, public health initiatives, substance abuse prevention, and administrative costs, to ADE, SBE, the department of public safety and the attorney general for mandatory administrative expenditures of state revenues required by the proposition. 2. Require that if any portion of the measure is deemed invalid, the remainder of the proposition shall be unaffected, and the invalid provisions shall be interpreted to the greatest extent possible allowed under the law. 3. Designate this proposition as the "Protect Education Act."

- 1 - PROPOSITION ___ [HCR 2021 - 2025] food; municipal tax; exemption ANALYSIS BY LEGISLATIVE COUNCIL Proposition ___ would limit the ability of a city, town or other taxing jurisdiction to impose a transaction privilege, sales, use, franchise or other similar tax or fee on food and certain nonalcoholic beverages (ready-to-drink and in a closed container) that are intended for home consumption as follows: 1. For a city, town or other taxing jurisdiction that approved the imposition of such a tax or fee on or before January 1, 2025, any increase in the rate of the tax or fee must be approved by the voters and may not be more than two percent of the tax base. However, if the rate of the tax or fee imposed on or before January 1, 2025 is two percent or more of the tax base, the city, town or other taxing jurisdiction may not increase the rate. Additionally, increases in the rate of the tax or fee may not occur between June 30, 2025 and June 30, 2027. 2. For a city, town or other taxing jurisdiction that has not approved the imposition of such a tax or fee on or before January 1, 2025, the adoption of a new tax or fee and any subsequent increase to the rate of the tax or fee must be approved by the voters and may not be more than two percent of the tax base. Additionally, the adoption of a new tax or fee and any subsequent increase to the rate of the tax or fee may not occur between June 30, 2025 and June 30, 2027.

- 1 - PROPOSITION __ [HCR 2055 - 2025] drug cartels; terrorist organizations ANALYSIS BY LEGISLATIVE COUNCIL Proposition ___ would declare that drug cartels (associations of persons engaging in human smuggling, drug trafficking for profit or any act of terrorism) are terrorist organizations. The proposition would: 1. Require the Arizona Department of Homeland Security to use all lawful means available within its authority to address threats posed by drug cartels. 2. Declare that this proposition does not support an alien's claim for asylum under federal law.

- 1 - PROPOSITION ___ [HCR 2003 - 2026] interscholastic; intramural athletics; biological sex ANALYSIS BY LEGISLATIVE COUNCIL Proposition ___ would prohibit males from playing in female interscholastic and intramural sports based on the biological sex of the participating athletes as recorded at birth on the athletes' original birth certificates. This proposition would amend Arizona law to require public and private schools and athletic associations that sponsor an interscholastic or intramural athletic team or sport to expressly designate such teams and sports as "males", "men", "boys", "females", "women", "girls", "coeducational" or "mixed". Proposition ___ would also: 1. Prohibit public schools, private schools, higher education institutions and athletic associations that provide and maintain private spaces, including restrooms, locker rooms and shower rooms, that are integral to athletic engagement from authorizing any individual to use a private space that is not designated for that individual's biological sex as recorded at birth on the individual's original birth certificate. 2. Expand who may sue and be sued for alleged violations of the law. 3. Provide that this proposition would not restrict any athlete's eligibility to participate on a team or in a sport that is aligned with the athlete's sex or that is designated as "coeducational" or "mixed". 4. Define the term "athlete" to include students and individuals who participate in any athletic team or sport. 5. Designate this proposition as the "Protect Girls' Sports in Arizona Act."
analyses.measureTitle: Proposition 318: Interscholastic; intramural athletics; biological sex

analyses.text: - 1 - PROPOSITION __ [SCR 1004 - 2026] photo enforcement systems; voter approval ANALYSIS BY LEGISLATIVE COUNCIL Legislative Council Staff Draft Proposition ___ would prohibit a local authority or state agency from using a photo 1 enforcement system for speeding or traffic control device violations unless the local authority or 2 state agency has a contract in place before December 31, 2026 to operate a photo enforcement 3 system. If the local authority has a photo enforcement system contract in place before December 4 31, 2026, Proposition ___ would require the local authority to seek approval from the voters at the 5 next general election to continue to operate the photo enforcement system. If the voters fail to 6 approve the continued operation of the existing photo enforcement system, Proposition ___ would 7 require that the local authority cease operations of the photo enforcement system within 90 days 8 after the election. If the voters approve the continued operation of the existing photo enforcement 9 system, Proposition ___ would allow the continued operation of the photo enforcement system for 10 a period of 10 years. At the conclusion of each 10-year period, the local authority must seek 11 approval from the voters for the continued operation of the photo enforcement system for a period 12 of an additional 10 years. 13

analyses.text: - 1 - PROPOSITION ___ [SCR 1032 - 2026] instructional expenses; operational spending; enforcement ANALYSIS BY LEGISLATIVE COUNCIL Proposition ___ would require each school district that has a student count of at least 7,500 or that operates a school in a county with a population of at least 500,000 persons to spend at least 60 percent of the school district's operational spending on direct instructional expenses. The proposition would require the auditor general to define "direct instructional expenses" and "operational spending" for the purposes of this requirement. Beginning in fiscal year 2027-2028, Proposition ___ would require any school district that spends less than 60 percent of the school district's operational spending on direct instructional expenses to increase the portion of the school district's operational spending that is spent on direct instructional expenses each year by at least one-half of one percent per year until the school district is in compliance. If a school district does not comply with these requirements, this proposition would require the Arizona Department of Education to reduce the school district's allocation from the classroom site fund for the budget year by 25 percent of the amount that would otherwise be allocated to the school district from the classroom site fund for each year the school district did not comply, up to a maximum of 100 percent of the amount if the school district did not comply for four or more years, unless a waiver is granted. Monies that are not distributed because of reductions would be allocated to compliant school districts for the following school year.

Official statewide canvass of the July 21, 2026 primary, certified August 6, 2026, 13 pages. Read the full document by OCR and matched starred congressional and legislative nominees against the official November voter guide and September 24 captured official candidate listing. The canvass supplies all nine congressional primary nominee lists. Qualified November write-ins are separately sourced from the September 9 official list. The non-authoritative cross-check capture is https://politicalmediamonitor.com/api/politicians/p_gzvszbz11/files/17221?download=1 (41 pages, saved separately); no published fact relies on that capture alone.

Official November 3, 2026 general-election Voter Education Guide, linked from https://azcleanelections.gov/voter-education-guide. Extracted all 60 legislative contest rosters and 158 named candidates, including candidates whose statements read None Provided; matched nominee names and party to the Secretary of State primary canvass. Nick Fierro is an independent general-election candidate listed in the guide and is not a primary nominee. Added the 54 legislative district contests absent from the saved ballot and verified missing nominees in existing contests; retained existing ballot entries and their original sources. Qualified write-ins come from the Secretary of State separate official list.

November 3, 2026 General Election Write-In and Withdrawn Candidates, revised September 9, 2026, linked as https://azsos.gov/media/718 by the Secretary of State election page. Contains 15 qualified write-ins: seven U.S. House, four legislative, and four statewide candidates; states no withdrawn candidates. All write-ins in the newly added district races are included. Existing candidate rows and their original sources are retained; newly verified missing general candidates are added.
